newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-U.S. Sept housing starts seen declining.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-U.S. Sept housing starts seen declining.

text.p: U.S. housing starts tapered off in September to a moderate pace with higher interest rates still acting as only a minimal restraint on activity in that sector of the economy, economists believe.

The government will report housing starts on Thursday, October 17 at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. Economists polled by Reuters offered an average estimate of 1.47 million starts on an annualized basis, down from an annualized 1.525 million in August.
"Based on the home builders survey, housing starts is going to be a soft report," said Waldo Best, senior economist at BZW Securities.
The National Association of Home Builders said on Wednesday that its Housing Market Index fell three points to 53 in October from 56 in September.
Builders' ratings of single-family home sales fell to 57 in October from 60 in September.
Traffic of prospective buyers fell to 41 from 43. The component index for single family sales in the next six months fell to 60 from 62, it said.

"We've been using the Home Builders survey as a leading indicator for housing starts," said Best. "Whenever the homebuilders' survey softens up, it tends to be accompanied by softness in housing starts as well."
Best is looking for September housing starts to total an annualized 1.45 million.

"We are looking for some pullback from the strength you saw in August," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds. "That reflects the fact that (new housing construction) permits came off in August."
Flanagan said hurricane weather in September also acted as a restraint on housing starts.
Flanagan was skeptical of the monthly correlation between the Home Builders survey and the U.S. housing starts data.
"Over time, they move in the same direction, but on a month-to-month basis, there hasn't been a good correlation recently," he said.
Flanagan said a pullback in September housing starts "wouldn't come as a surprise to anybody."
He said housing activity remains fairly strong, "especially against the backdrop of rising rates."
Best said the housing market seems to have been able to accommodate the higher interest rates.

"It looks like there was a lot of pipeline mortgage activity in the summer that was insulated from higher rates, (financing that was) nailed to the front end of the (yield) curve," said Best. "That has allowed this miniboom in housing to continue. A lot of people in the real estate sector expected (even) higher rates and when that didn't happen, a lot of people continued to be active."
